tagline: Endless steppe and a working spaceport
overview:
Kazakhstan is the world's largest landlocked country and the ninth largest overall, bigger than all of Western Europe put together, yet only about 20 million people live there. It reaches from the Caspian Sea in the west to the mountains bordering China in the east, and from Siberia in the north to Central Asian deserts in the south. Astana, the capital, is a young, sharply modern city on the northern steppe with bitterly cold winters.

Kazakh and Russian are both official languages; Kazakh is a Turkic language, and the country is shifting its alphabet from Cyrillic to Latin letters. Kazakhstan is a republic. Oil, gas, uranium and metals make it the wealthiest country in Central Asia, and it mines more uranium than anywhere else on Earth. Almaty, the largest city, sits beneath snowy mountains in the southeast and served as the capital until 1997, when the government moved north.
landAndNature: Most of Kazakhstan is steppe, grassland so flat and open that the horizon can look like the sea, and it forms the largest dry steppe region in the world. The south holds desert and the shrunken Aral Sea, once the fourth largest lake on Earth until Soviet irrigation diverted the rivers feeding it, leaving rusting ships stranded on dry sand. Snow-capped Tian Shan peaks rise in the southeast, where Khan Tengri tops 6,995 meters. Saiga antelope, with bulging noses that filter dust and warm freezing air, migrate across the plains in enormous herds, and snow leopards hunt in the mountains, where wild apple trees still grow.
peopleAndCulture: Horses are central to Kazakh life: people ride them, race them, and drink kumis, fermented mare's milk that is sharp and slightly fizzy. Beshbarmak, meaning five fingers, is the national dish of boiled meat and wide noodles eaten by hand. Families still raise yurts, round felt tents, for weddings and summer camps. Kazakhs are known for hunting with golden eagles, riding out in winter with the huge birds on their arms to catch foxes and hares. The dombra, a two-stringed lute, accompanies long sung stories. Nauryz, the spring new year in March, brings feasting, games and horseback contests.
history: Nomadic horse peoples have crossed these grasslands for thousands of years, and researchers believe horses were first tamed in this region. Scythian burial mounds yielded a warrior's suit covered in thousands of gold pieces, known as the Golden Man. Silk Road caravans passed through southern cities such as Turkistan. Genghis Khan's armies swept in during the 1200s, and Kazakh khanates formed by the 1400s. The Russian Empire took control in the 1800s, and under Soviet rule in the 1930s forced collectivization caused a famine that killed a large share of the Kazakh population. The Soviets also tested nuclear weapons near Semipalatinsk. Kazakhstan became independent in 1991 and closed the test site.
funFacts: Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan launched the first satellite and the first human into space, and rockets still lift off there.
Kazakhstan is the largest landlocked country in the world, bigger than all of Western Europe combined.
Kazakhstan mines more uranium than any other country, supplying much of the world's nuclear fuel.
Wild apples still grow in the mountains near Almaty, and scientists trace the cultivated apple back to them.
The Aral Sea shrank so far that fishing boats were left sitting on sand many kilometers from any water.
